practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a health-related component of fitness?
A) Agility
B) Reaction time
C) Muscular strength
D) Coordination
practice_questions.marks: C) Muscular strength [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two skill-related components of fitness.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: speed / power / agility / balance / coordination / reaction time. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by aerobic endurance and give one example of a sport where it is particularly important.
practice_questions.marks: A basic definition scores 1 mark (e.g. "the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to muscles during exercise"). A developed definition scores 2 marks (e.g. "the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period, delaying fatigue"). A clear, relevant sporting example scores the third mark (e.g. "marathon running, where the performer must sustain effort for over 2 hours"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by agility and explain why it is important for a basketball player.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): agility is the ability to change body position or direction quickly and accurately while maintaining balance and control (2 marks for a complete, precise description; 1 mark for a partial definition such as "changing direction quickly" without reference to control or balance).
Explanation of importance (up to 2 marks): for example, a basketball player must constantly change direction to evade defenders or close down opponents on the court — without high agility they would lose possession more easily and be unable to create scoring opportunities (2 marks for a developed, sport-specific explanation; 1 mark for a vague statement such as "it helps them move around the court"). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A hockey goalkeeper is preparing for an important cup final. Their coach has identified reaction time and power as the two most important components of fitness for their position.

Discuss how each component benefits the goalkeeper's performance during a match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A developed discussion covering both components with clear sporting context. Reaction time: the goalkeeper must respond instantly to a shot or deflection from a short distance — faster reaction time means they can begin their movement before the ball has covered half the distance, making saves that would be impossible for a slower responder. Power: a goal kick or aerial clearance requires explosive leg and arm drive to send the ball the length of the pitch to relieve pressure; a goalkeeper with greater power can clear danger more efficiently. The answer identifies specific moments in a match where each component is decisive. Mastering answers may also note that both components interact — a fast reaction means little if the goalkeeper lacks the explosive power to reach the ball in time.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both components addressed with basic justification.
Developing (2 marks): One component addressed with limited justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A 400-metre runner and a gymnastics floor performer both compete at a high level. Compare the components of fitness that are most important for each performer, and evaluate which performer needs a broader range of fitness components to succeed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced comparison identifying key components for each. 400-metre runner: aerobic endurance (sustaining effort over ~45-50 seconds), muscular endurance (repeated stride cycle), speed (maintaining top velocity in the final 100 metres), reaction time (leaving the blocks quickly). Gymnastics floor: flexibility (splits, extensions), balance (holding static positions and landing from tumbles), coordination (linking complex movement sequences), power (propelling tumbles and leaps). Evaluation: gymnastics demands a wider range of components because the routine must demonstrate flexibility, balance, coordination, power and strength within a single performance; the 400-metre runner demands high levels of fewer components but at a more extreme level. Substantiated judgement with justification.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two components for each performer with an attempt at evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Components identified for both, limited comparison.
Emerging (1-2 marks): One or two relevant points with no comparison or evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a personal factor that must be considered before designing a training programme?
A) The quality of the gym equipment
B) The performer's lifestyle
C) The size of the sports hall
D) The weather on training days
practice_questions.marks: B) The performer's lifestyle [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two personal factors a coach must consider before starting a training programme with a new performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: health / fitness / age / gender / lifestyle / time available for training / cost of training. Answers that list the same factor twice score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why completing a PAR-Q is important before a new performer starts a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'it checks for health issues'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'it identifies medical conditions such as a heart problem that could make vigorous exercise dangerous, allowing the coach to seek medical clearance first'). A further developed point or a second distinct reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'it also protects the coach professionally — if a performer has a health event during training and no screening was completed, the coach may be liable'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A coach is designing a training programme for a 45-year-old recreational tennis player who has a part-time job and can only train three times per week.

Describe two factors the coach should consider before writing the programme.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks available per factor (1 for identifying the factor, 1 for explaining its relevance to this specific performer). For example: age (1) — at 45 the performer will have reduced muscle elasticity and require more recovery time between sessions, so the programme must include adequate rest days (1); time available (1) — only three sessions per week limits total training volume, so each session must be well-targeted at the components most relevant to tennis (1). Accept any two relevant factors with applied explanation. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old student wants to improve her performance in the 800 m. She has mild asthma and attends school five days a week. She can train four evenings per week at a local running track and has access to a school gym.

Discuss the factors a coach should consider before designing a training programme for this performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A thorough discussion covering personal factors (medical condition — asthma affects safe exercise intensity and may require an inhaler protocol; age — growing body, appropriate resistance loading; time available — four evenings, realistic volume; current fitness level — baseline testing needed) and environmental factors (running track and school gym — enables both cardiovascular and strength work). SMART goal-setting referenced: e.g. 'improve 800 m time from 3:20 to 3:05 by the end of term' shows all five criteria. Interaction between factors noted — e.g. asthma and intensity constraints must be reflected in the measurable and realistic elements of the SMART target.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least three factors identified with some explanation and partial application to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Two factors identified but explanation is superficial.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A newly qualified coach is planning a training programme for a group of adult beginners at a local leisure centre. The group includes participants aged 18-55, one of whom has recently had a knee operation and another who is a smoker with high blood pressure.

Evaluate how effectively the coach can design a safe and appropriate training programme given the range of personal and environmental factors present in this scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates both the breadth of personal factors (wide age range requires differentiated intensity; medical conditions — post-surgery knee and high blood pressure — demand PAR-Q completion and possible medical clearance before these individuals train; lifestyle factor of smoking reduces cardiovascular efficiency) and environmental factors (leisure centre likely provides good facilities, but coach must check equipment suitability and space for the group size). SMART goals must be set individually within the group context. The challenge of designing one programme that meets all needs is weighed against the option of sub-grouping. A substantiated judgement is given — e.g. the coach can design a safe programme but must conduct individual health screening, set differentiated targets and build a thorough risk assessment into every session; the wide variance in personal factors makes a single-plan approach insufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): Multiple personal and environmental factors identified and applied to the scenario; an attempt at evaluative judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant factors listed with some explanation; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a ball and socket joint?
A) The knee
B) The elbow
C) The shoulder
D) The wrist
practice_questions.marks: C) The shoulder [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two major voluntary muscles found in the lower body.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: quadriceps / hamstrings / gastrocnemius / gluteus maximus. Answers must name a muscle from the required list to score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of the trachea and explain why this structure is important during exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Description (1 mark): the trachea is a tube running from the larynx that divides into the bronchi, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. Explanation (up to 2 marks): the cartilage rings keep the airway open even when the neck moves during exercise, ensuring a constant flow of air to the lungs (1 mark for stating the cartilage keeps the airway open; 2 marks for adding that this prevents collapse under the pressure changes of vigorous breathing). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the journey of blood through the four chambers of the heart, naming the key blood vessels involved.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of the following, to a maximum of 4: deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium via the vena cava; passes into the right ventricle; is pumped to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; returns oxygenated to the left atrium via the pulmonary vein; passes into the left ventricle; is pumped to the body via the aorta. (Award up to 4 of these marks; a complete, ordered response scores 4 marks.) [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old football player is told by her coach that her explosive sprinting is linked to her muscle fibre composition. Using your knowledge of muscle fibre types, explain how the structure of Type I and Type II fibres makes them suited to different sporting demands.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both fibre types with structural reasons linked clearly to sporting demands. For example: Type I (slow-twitch) fibres are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, enabling sustained aerobic energy production — well suited to endurance activities such as a goalkeeper's repeated repositioning or a midfielder's 90-minute work rate. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres lack high mitochondrial density but have rapid cross-bridge cycling and access to large anaerobic energy stores, enabling explosive short bursts such as a sprint to the ball. The answer links structural features (mitochondria, contraction speed) to function and gives sporting examples.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both types identified and their general characteristics described, with some link to sport.
Developing (2 marks): One type described with limited sporting link.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic statement about fast and slow fibres with no structural detail. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sport scientist is assessing two athletes: a long-distance runner and a javelin thrower. Using your knowledge of the structure of the skeletal, muscular and cardiovascular systems, evaluate how the structural features of these systems combine to support performance in each athlete's chosen sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced, system-linked evaluation covering all three systems for both athlete types. For the distance runner: dense capillary networks around Type I fibres maximise oxygen delivery; synovial joints (especially hinge joints at the knee) allow repetitive extension-flexion without dislocation; long bones of the lower limb act as efficient levers; the heart's left ventricle pumps blood continuously to working muscles. For the javelin thrower: upper-body muscles (deltoids, pectorals, triceps, latissimus dorsi) generate the throwing force; ball and socket joint at the shoulder permits the circumduction needed for the run-up and release; Type II fibres in the throwing arm produce rapid, powerful contractions; the cardiovascular system recovers between throws. Substantiated conclusion about why neither athlete could perform without the integration of all three systems.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two systems addressed for both athletes, with relevant structural points and some evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely descriptive; limited cross-system links.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic recall of individual structures with no evaluation or athlete application. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the principle of specificity?
A) Training load must be increased gradually over time
B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role
C) Different training sessions should be used to prevent boredom
D) Each athlete requires a different amount of rest between sessions
practice_questions.marks: B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the four components of the FITT principle.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct components: Frequency / Intensity / Time / Type. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the principle of reversibility and give one sporting example of when it would apply.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): reversibility is the loss of fitness adaptations when training is reduced or stopped. Explanation (1 mark): e.g. the body no longer needs to maintain the higher fitness level so cardiovascular endurance, strength and flexibility decline. Sporting example (1 mark): e.g. a swimmer who is ill for three weeks will return to training with a noticeably lower aerobic capacity and will need to rebuild their programme gradually. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A coach is planning a ten-week training programme for a 16-year-old club tennis player who currently trains twice a week for 30 minutes. Describe how the coach could use the FITT principle to apply progressive overload over the ten weeks.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks — one mark per FITT component correctly applied with an appropriate progression example: Frequency (e.g. increase from 2 to 3 sessions per week by week 5); Intensity (e.g. introduce high-intensity drills and reduce rest periods between rallies); Time (e.g. extend sessions from 30 to 45 minutes); Type (e.g. add in agility ladder work and plyometric drills alongside court-based practice). Answers that simply name the four components without applying them score a maximum of 2 marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A football coach has been running the same three sessions every week for the past two months. Several players have reported feeling bored and their fitness test scores have stopped improving.

Discuss how applying the principles of training could address these problems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least three principles with clear application to the scenario. For example: the plateau in fitness scores indicates that progressive overload has not been applied — the coach should increase frequency, intensity, time or type using the FITT principle to provide a new stimulus. The player boredom reflects a failure to apply variance — rotating between circuit training, fartlek sessions and small-sided games would reduce tedium and maintain motivation. Individual needs should also be considered — some players may have plateaued because the current sessions are too easy for their fitness level while others are struggling.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two principles identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One principle identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sprint athlete has been training consistently for six months and has improved their 60-metre time from 8.4 seconds to 7.9 seconds. They then sustain a soft-tissue injury and are advised to rest completely for four weeks.

Evaluate the likely impact of this rest period on the athlete's fitness, and explain how the coach should plan the return to training using the principles of training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Reversibility correctly applied — cardiovascular endurance declines within 2-3 weeks; neuromuscular adaptations (speed, power) also diminish; four weeks of complete rest means a significant reduction in anaerobic capacity and fast-twitch muscle conditioning. Return-to-training plan uses multiple principles: individual needs (assess current fitness before resuming, not assuming previous level); progressive overload via FITT (begin at reduced intensity and duration, gradually rebuilding over 2-4 weeks); specificity (sprint-specific work — acceleration drills and block starts — reintroduced progressively); variance (initial sessions may include cross-training to maintain general fitness without stressing the injury site before full sprint training resumes); rest and recovery (adequate recovery between sessions to allow tissue repair). A substantiated judgement — e.g. the reversal of six months' gains within four weeks highlights why managing return-to-training systematically is critical, and why coaches must monitor fitness test scores post-return rather than assuming full recovery.
Secure (5-6 marks): Reversibility explained and return plan covers at least two principles applied to the scenario.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points mostly descriptive with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a function of the skeletal system?
A) Gaseous exchange
B) Blood-cell production
C) Vasodilation
D) Antagonistic action
practice_questions.marks: B) Blood-cell production [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two functions of the muscular system during sport and exercise.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct functions from: movement through contraction / agonist-antagonist action; maintaining posture; generating heat. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the cardiovascular system regulates body temperature during vigorous exercise.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'blood vessels widen'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'vasodilation causes blood vessels near the skin surface to widen, bringing warm blood to the surface where heat is lost to the environment'). A third mark is awarded for also mentioning vasoconstriction as the opposing mechanism used when the body needs to retain heat, or for explaining the role of the autonomic nervous system in controlling both processes. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of gaseous exchange that occurs in the respiratory system during exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the alveoli as the site of exchange (1); oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood (capillaries) due to a concentration gradient (1); carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the alveoli (1); CO2 is then expelled during expiration while oxygenated blood is transported to working muscles by the cardiovascular system (1). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A football player is sprinting at high intensity during the second half of a match. Using your knowledge of two body systems, explain how the body responds to meet the increased demand for oxygen in the working muscles.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both the cardiovascular system (heart rate and stroke volume increase to raise cardiac output; more oxygenated blood delivered per minute; vasodilation redirects blood to working muscles) and the respiratory system (breathing rate and tidal volume increase; more oxygen reaches alveoli; gaseous exchange rate increases via diffusion). Clear link between both systems and the specific demand of the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both systems identified with reasonable explanation but limited application to the sprint scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One system explained, or both identified without explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
During a bicep curl exercise, identify the agonist and antagonist muscles acting at the elbow joint during the upward phase. Explain the antagonistic action taking place and describe one other function of the muscular system that occurs during this movement.

A weightlifter is lifting a heavy barbell overhead in a cold gym. Discuss how two body systems respond to support this performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Part 1 — biceps = agonist (contracts to flex the elbow, pulling the forearm upward); triceps = antagonist (relaxes to allow the movement). Antagonistic action explained clearly (agonist shortens, antagonist lengthens). Second muscular function: e.g. fixator muscles stabilise the shoulder joint; core muscles maintain posture; heat is generated as a by-product of contraction (any one with brief explanation). Part 2 — musculoskeletal: bones act as levers at the shoulder, elbow and wrist joints, with muscles attached via tendons pulling on these levers to create upward movement; skeletal function of protection (ribcage/spine under load). Cardiovascular: vasoconstriction in a cold environment to retain heat; increased cardiac output to deliver oxygen and nutrients to working muscles. Both systems applied to the weightlifting context with a substantiated judgement about which system is most critical.
Secure (5-6 marks): Agonist/antagonist correctly identified, second function noted, two systems explained with reasonable application.
Developing (3-4 marks): Partial credit on antagonistic action, one system explained.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which fitness test is used to measure agility?
A) Stork stand
B) Ruler drop test
C) Illinois agility run
D) Vertical jump test
practice_questions.marks: C) Illinois agility run [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
State the fitness test used to measure each of the following components:
(a) Aerobic endurance
(b) Balance
practice_questions.marks: (a) One mark for either: multistage fitness test (bleep test / 20-metre shuttle run) OR Cooper 12-minute run. (b) One mark for: stork stand (stork balance test). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the protocol for the ruler drop test, used to measure reaction time.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per valid protocol point up to 3 marks from: tester holds ruler vertically at 0 cm between participant's open thumb and forefinger (1) / tester drops ruler without warning and participant catches it as quickly as possible (1) / the distance the ruler falls is recorded in centimetres and converted to milliseconds using a conversion table (1) / several trials are taken and the average used (1). Maximum 3 marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the validity and reliability of a fitness test.
practice_questions.marks: Validity (up to 2 marks): a test is valid if it actually measures the component it claims to measure, e.g. the sit-and-reach is a valid measure of lower-back and hamstring flexibility (2 marks for definition + example; 1 mark for definition alone). Reliability (up to 2 marks): a test is reliable if repeated testing under the same conditions produces consistent results, e.g. if warm-up, equipment and instructions change between tests the results cannot be reliably compared (2 marks for definition + consequence; 1 mark for definition alone). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sports coach wants to test the muscular strength and aerobic endurance of a group of 16-year-old athletes before designing their training programme.

Describe an appropriate fitness test for each component and explain how the results could be used.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two tests described with clear protocol detail and clear explanation of use. Strength: grip dynamometer test — participant squeezes as hard as possible, best of three attempts recorded in kilograms, compared to normative data to rate the athlete's strength relative to their age group; result provides a baseline and identifies whether strength training is a priority. Aerobic endurance: multistage fitness test — participant runs 20-metre shuttles in time with progressive beeps, level and shuttle reached recorded and compared to normative data; result highlights cardiovascular fitness and informs target training zones. Both tests must be reliable (same conditions each time) and valid to allow meaningful comparison with normative data.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both tests named with some protocol detail and some explanation of use.
Developing (2 marks): One test described adequately or both named without protocol detail.
Emerging (1 mark): One test named only. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A female 400-metre runner scores 14.3 seconds on the Illinois agility run and 38 cm on the vertical jump test. Her coach notes that both scores fall in the 'below average' band for her age group according to normative data tables.

Evaluate how useful normative data is for measuring and improving this athlete's fitness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced evaluation of the usefulness of normative data with specific reference to the scenario. Arguments for usefulness: scores below average for agility and power give the coach objective targets; normative data provides a standardised benchmark allowing comparison across athletes; helps prioritise which components to train first. Arguments against or limitations: normative data may not reflect the specific demands of 400-metre running — agility may not be a priority component; general population tables may not be appropriate for elite-level comparisons (athlete-specific normative data is better); if testing conditions were not fully standardised the comparison is unreliable; normative data shows where the athlete stands but does not explain why or how to improve. Substantiated judgement: normative data is a useful starting point for identifying areas below the expected range, but its value depends entirely on the validity and reliability of the test — coaches should use it alongside sport-specific performance data rather than in isolation.
Secure (5-6 marks): Clear points on both sides with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mainly one-sided with limited reference to scenario.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about normative data with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which training method involves exercising at a constant, moderate pace for an extended period without rest?
A) Interval training
B) Fartlek training
C) Continuous training
D) Circuit training
practice_questions.marks: C) Continuous training [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of fartlek training for a football player.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: it develops both aerobic and anaerobic fitness / it replicates the unpredictable intensity changes of match play / it is varied and reduces boredom / it is flexible as the performer decides when to increase pace / it can be performed on any terrain without specialist equipment. Answers must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the work-to-rest ratio in interval training can be adapted to target different energy systems.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "shorter rest targets the anaerobic system"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a short work period with long rest — such as 20 seconds effort, 2 minutes rest — stresses the anaerobic ATP-PC system, developing explosive speed"). A further developed or second mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "longer, moderate-intensity intervals with shorter rest, such as 3 minutes work with 1 minute rest, keep heart rate elevated in the aerobic zone and develop cardiovascular endurance"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between static stretching and PNF stretching, and explain why PNF can produce greater flexibility gains.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): static stretching involves holding a muscle at its end range for 15–30 seconds without movement (1 mark); PNF involves contracting the stretched muscle isometrically then relaxing and deepening the stretch with the help of a partner (1 mark). Explanation of PNF advantage (up to 2 marks): the isometric contraction temporarily fatigues the motor neurones (1 mark), which suppresses the stretch reflex and allows the muscle to lengthen further in the relaxation phase, achieving a greater range of motion than static stretching alone (1 mark for developed mechanism). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A strength and conditioning coach is designing a 6-week pre-season programme for a basketball team. The coach wants to improve both explosive jumping power and cardiovascular fitness.

Discuss which two training methods the coach should select and justify each choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two clearly identified methods (e.g. plyometric training and HIIT/interval training) with developed justification linked to basketball demands. Plyometrics: develops power through the stretch-shortening cycle; box jumps and depth jumps directly replicate the explosive jumping required for rebounds and shot-blocking (2 marks for developed justification). HIIT or interval training: develops cardiovascular fitness time-efficiently; short sprint intervals replicate the high-intensity bursts of basketball where players sprint, stop and sprint repeatedly throughout a 40-minute game (2 marks for developed justification). A comment on how the two methods complement each other scores the final mark.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two methods identified, justified with some reference to basketball.
Developing (2 marks): One method identified with some justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant method named without justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A long-distance cyclist wants to improve their cardiovascular endurance over a 16-week training block. They currently only use continuous training.

Evaluate the extent to which adding HIIT sessions would improve their performance more than continuing with continuous training alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing both sides. For HIIT: research suggests HIIT can produce equivalent or superior cardiovascular adaptations in less time; the high intensity stresses both aerobic and anaerobic systems, improving lactate threshold and VO2 max more rapidly; variety reduces boredom and psychological fatigue from long sessions. Against / limitations of HIIT: continuous training builds the aerobic base essential for event-specific endurance; HIIT sessions are very demanding and recovery must be managed to avoid overtraining; a cyclist who races for 3+ hours needs sustained moderate-intensity endurance that HIIT alone cannot fully replicate. Substantiated judgement: a combined approach (periodised mix of continuous and HIIT) is most effective — HIIT for adaptations, continuous training for race-specific endurance.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides addressed with some evidence/reasoning; some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or limited development.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a 'baseline' in fitness testing?
A) A comparison of results against normative data tables
B) An initial set of test results recorded before a training programme begins
C) A target set by the coach for the performer to reach
D) The average score across all components of fitness
practice_questions.marks: B) An initial set of test results recorded before a training programme begins [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why a coach would carry out fitness testing with a performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct reasons from the specification list: to compare against normative data / to identify strengths and weaknesses / to provide a baseline for future comparisons / to provide important information for the coach / to assist team selection / to set goals or targets. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'normative data' and how a coach can use it when analysing a performer's fitness test results.
practice_questions.marks: A simple definition scores 1 mark (e.g. 'normative data is average scores for a fitness test'). Development that includes the age/gender categories and how performance is rated (poor/average/above average/excellent) scores 2 marks. A further developed explanation covering how the coach uses normative data — for example, to judge whether the performer's score is sufficient for their sport, or to identify which components need improvement relative to peers — scores 3 marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A coach records a 15-year-old footballer's multistage fitness test score as level 9.4. Write one SMART target for this performer, explaining how the target meets the SMART criteria.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating a plausible target (e.g. 'reach level 10.2 on the multistage fitness test within 8 weeks'). One mark each for explaining how the target is specific, measurable, achievable/realistic and time-phased — up to 3 further marks (any three of the four SMART elements clearly applied). A target that is clearly impractical (e.g. 'reach level 15 in 2 weeks') cannot score the achievable/realistic mark. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why both validity and reliability are important when a coach carries out fitness testing with a sports performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Validity and reliability are each defined correctly (validity = measuring the right component; reliability = consistency of results under the same conditions). Their importance is explained with developed reasoning: without validity the test does not measure what the coach thinks it does, making comparisons with normative data meaningless; without reliability, repeated test scores cannot be trusted as evidence of real improvement. The answer applies these ideas to coaching practice (e.g. choosing an appropriate protocol, standardising conditions).
Secure (3-4 marks): Both terms defined and their importance briefly explained.
Developing (2 marks): One term defined with some explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic point about one term, no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A basketball coach is planning a new six-week training programme for her squad. Evaluate how fitness testing before, during and after the programme can benefit both the coach and her players.

In your answer, refer to at least three reasons for fitness testing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): At least three reasons from the specification are discussed with developed evaluation. Example points: baseline testing identifies individual strengths and weaknesses before the programme begins, allowing the coach to personalise the training plan rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach; mid-programme re-testing allows the coach to adapt the programme if progress is slower than expected; comparing results to normative data shows how players compare to peers and helps with team selection for competitive fixtures; SMART targets set from baseline data motivate players by giving them specific, measurable goals to aim at; post-programme testing shows whether the six-week block produced the intended adaptations. A well-developed answer evaluates the relative importance of these reasons (e.g. arguing that the motivational benefit is only effective if tests are reliable and if SMART targets are realistic).
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two reasons discussed with some evaluation and reference to the scenario.
Developing (3-4 marks): Two or more reasons stated but explanation is limited and evaluation is absent.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points, one reason, no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines cardiac output?
A) The number of times the heart beats per minute
B) The volume of blood pumped per beat
C) Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
D) The volume of air breathed in per minute
practice_questions.marks: C) Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two short-term effects of exercise on the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of the following: increased heart rate / increased stroke volume / increased cardiac output / vasodilation (redirection of blood to working muscles) / increase in body temperature. Maximum 2 marks. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why breathing rate and tidal volume both increase during exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that working muscles require more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. 1 mark for explaining that breathing rate increases to move air in and out more frequently, and 1 mark for explaining that tidal volume increases so each breath takes in a larger volume of air — together raising minute ventilation to meet the greater demand. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how blood flow is redirected to the working muscles during exercise and explain why this is important.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): blood vessels supplying the working muscles vasodilate (widen) while vessels to less active organs vasoconstrict (narrow); this redistributes the increased cardiac output towards the areas of greatest need (2 marks for both vasodilation and vasoconstriction with correct application; 1 mark for one mechanism only).
Explanation (up to 2 marks): increased blood flow delivers more oxygen and nutrients to the working muscles, enabling continued energy production and delaying fatigue (2 marks for a developed explanation linking blood flow to muscle function; 1 mark for a basic statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 400m sprinter crosses the finish line breathing very heavily and with a burning sensation in both legs. She is unable to sprint again for several minutes.

Using your knowledge of the short-term effects of exercise on body systems, explain the physiological reasons for her symptoms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation covering at least three linked short-term effects applied to the scenario. For example: during a 400m sprint the cardiovascular system increases heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output to maximise oxygen delivery; however, at sprint intensity the cardio-respiratory system cannot supply oxygen quickly enough, so the muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid; lactic acid accumulates faster than it can be cleared, causing the burning sensation and muscle fatigue that prevents her from sprinting again; elevated body temperature triggers increased sweating and vasodilation near the skin; continued elevated heart rate and breathing rate post-race reflect the body's attempt to clear lactic acid through EPOC.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two short-term effects identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two effects named but not well linked to the symptoms.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sports coach is preparing a warm-up for a team before a training session. She gradually increases the intensity over five minutes.

Evaluate how the short-term effects of exercise during the warm-up benefit the performers when the full-intensity training begins.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation linking multiple short-term cardiovascular, respiratory and muscular effects to specific benefits. For example: gradually increasing heart rate and cardiac output ensures blood flow to muscles is already elevated before maximal effort begins; increased tidal volume means the respiratory system is primed and oxygen delivery is efficient from the start; rising muscle temperature increases elasticity, reducing injury risk and improving contraction speed; vasodilation is established, so muscles receive redirected blood flow immediately; sweating regulation mechanisms are activated, managing temperature before the heaviest work. Counter-argument: if warm-up is too intense too quickly, lactic acid builds up before full training begins, impeding performance from the outset. Substantiated judgement made.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least three effects with developed links to warm-up benefit and an attempt at evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Some relevant points, limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a long-term adaptation of regular endurance training on the cardiovascular system?
A) Increased resting heart rate
B) Decreased stroke volume
C) Cardiac hypertrophy
D) Reduced vital capacity
practice_questions.marks: C) Cardiac hypertrophy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two long-term adaptations of regular training on the musculoskeletal system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: muscle hypertrophy / increased bone density / stronger tendons and ligaments / muscular capillarisation / improved tolerance to lactic acid / increased muscular endurance or muscular strength. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a trained athlete has a lower resting heart rate than an untrained person of the same age.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. "the heart gets bigger"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "cardiac hypertrophy increases the size and strength of the left ventricle, so more blood is expelled per beat"). A full explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add "because each beat pumps a greater stroke volume, the heart needs to beat fewer times per minute to circulate the same volume of blood, producing bradycardia"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of capillarisation and explain how it benefits a sports performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): capillarisation is the growth of new capillary networks that occurs in two places — around the alveoli in the lungs and within the muscles themselves, as a result of regular training (2 marks for naming both locations; 1 mark for naming one location or a general description without locations).
Benefit (up to 2 marks): increased capillary density around the alveoli speeds up gas exchange — more oxygen diffuses into the blood per breath; increased capillary density in muscles improves oxygen and nutrient delivery and faster removal of carbon dioxide and waste products, delaying fatigue and improving performance (2 marks for a developed explanation with performance link; 1 mark for a basic benefit without development). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old sprinter has recently completed a six-month resistance and plyometric training programme. Her coach states that her body has undergone several long-term adaptations.

Discuss the long-term adaptations that her musculoskeletal system is likely to have undergone and explain how each will improve her sprint performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A developed discussion covering at least three musculoskeletal adaptations with clear links to sprint performance. For example: muscle hypertrophy (larger, stronger muscles generate more explosive force off the starting block and at each stride); increased bone density (denser bones withstand the high impact forces of sprinting, reducing fracture risk and allowing harder training); stronger tendons and ligaments (improve joint stability at the knee and ankle, allowing force to be transferred more efficiently during the push-off phase); improved lactic acid tolerance (allows repeated sprint efforts without early fatigue onset). Performance links are explicitly made and specific to sprinting.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two adaptations identified and explained with some performance application.
Developing (2 marks): One or two adaptations named but with limited explanation or no clear performance link.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A professional cyclist trains for 20 hours per week over several years. A sports scientist measures a resting heart rate of 42 bpm, vital capacity significantly above average, and very high muscular endurance.

Evaluate the extent to which long-term cardiovascular adaptations alone account for the cyclist's exceptional fitness, compared with adaptations in the respiratory and musculoskeletal systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying cardiovascular adaptations (cardiac hypertrophy → increased stroke volume → bradycardia of 42 bpm → faster recovery), respiratory adaptations (increased vital capacity, alveolar capillarisation, more efficient gas exchange), and musculoskeletal adaptations (muscular capillarisation, improved lactic acid tolerance, muscular endurance from mitochondrial density). The evaluation makes clear that cardiovascular adaptations are central — they underpin oxygen delivery — but cannot function independently of respiratory gas exchange or muscular oxygen utilisation. A substantiated judgement states that exceptional fitness results from all three systems adapting in concert; no single system explains the full picture. High-quality answers may note that the 20-hour weekly volume produces the depth of adaptation across all systems simultaneously.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two systems addressed with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly one-sided, or adaptations named without evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
